Even then, the cave's occupants did not collapse into one identity. Neanderthals and Denisovans both belonged to the wider history investigated at this remarkable archaeological site. There is no single percentage that describes every person everywhere. The interpretation involves interbreeding between ancestral populations. Over later generations, inherited segments were recombined and passed on within histories that included many other relationships and demographic changes. A surviving segment is not a complete Denisovan genome, and it is not a certificate of cultural identity. Biological inheritance answers a particular set of historical questions. Researchers compare how such segments resemble available ancient references. The results can suggest contacts and population structure without identifying every meeting place or reconstructing one exact journey. Studies have also found evidence for more than one Denisovan related contribution. A single Siberian reference cannot be assumed to represent every group involved in those contacts. This makes the cave both essential and incomplete. Its samples anchor comparisons, while the inherited record elsewhere points toward a wider diversity still needing direct evidence from fossils. One famous example concerns a region around a gene called EPAS1, involved in the body's response to low oxygen conditions at high altitude. Research published in 2014 linked a distinctive Tibetan version of this region with Denisovan or closely related ancestry, and with adaptation in a demanding environment. That finding is not a claim that one gene explains an entire population's abilities. Biological function, inherited variants, natural selection, and environmental conditions remain different parts of the explanation. Nor does a useful inherited variant prove that the individual from the Siberian cave personally lived on the Tibetan Plateau. An ancestral connection is not an individual biography. A direct fossil connection with the plateau would require another kind of evidence. That is where the story turns from DNA toward a different set of surviving molecules.
